lines.text: Your village needs water, but the river is a two hour walk away.
So you dig. Straight down, until the dirt turns dark and wet.
But the soft walls keep caving in.
So you line the hole with stones, stacked in a ring, each one wedged against the next.
Water seeps in through the gaps, but the walls hold. This is a well.
But the water sits thirty feet below you.
You tie a rope to a bucket and pull it up hand over hand, and by noon your palms are raw.
So you lay a log across the top and wind the rope around it.
Add a crank to one end, and every turn lifts the bucket a little higher. This is a windlass.
But a full bucket is heavy. Let go of the crank for one second, and it spins backward and the bucket crashes down.
So you cut teeth into a wheel on the axle and add a wooden peg that drops between them.
It clicks with every turn and catches the axle the moment you let go. This is a ratchet.
But leaves, dirt and the occasional frog keep falling in.
So you raise a little roof over it and lay a lid across the mouth.
But the first bucket of every morning tastes like mud.
So you pour a layer of gravel into the bottom, and the bucket stops stirring up mud.
Now anyone can draw clean water, right in the middle of the village.
Congratulations. You have built a well.
